title: Episode 1 - Optimizing Teacher Feedback: Coaching Over Criticism
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: The first instalment of a series on teacher feedback, built on a single ironic observation: the leadership teams who warn teachers against cognitively overloading students routinely overload their teachers with post-observation feedback. Emanuele describes the familiar experience of leaving a lesson that went well and receiving a list of 'missed' strategies - PP check-ins, vocabulary, retrieval, visible SEN support - several of which either happened outside the observed window or were wrong for that moment. His second argument is that feedback without modelling does not transfer, and he points to Steplab's Great Teaching Unpacked, where teachers and leaders role-play the feedback rather than merely naming it. That shift, he argues, turns feedback from something abstract and evaluative into something collaborative and developmental - coaching rather than criticism. The practical prescription is one actionable focus per observation, on the grounds that eight next steps dilute each other and none lands. He is careful not to make it an attack on leaders, framing the problem as well-intentioned schools accidentally producing the exact overload they train teachers to avoid.
points: The core argument is a consistency test for leadership: the cognitive-load principles schools impose on teacher-to-student instruction should govern leader-to-teacher feedback too.
Emanuele points out that observation feedback is generated from a small window, so 'you didn't do X' often means 'X did not happen in the ten minutes I watched' - or that X was wrong for that moment.
Live modelling and role-play of feedback, as in the Great Teaching Unpacked example, is offered as the mechanism that converts abstract advice into something a teacher can enact.
The concrete rule is one focus, not a list: anything beyond a single actionable next step adds load and dilutes impact.
He explicitly declines the easy villain, crediting leaders who care about wellbeing and locating the failure in eagerness to help rather than indifference.
quotes: Every teacher knows that post-observation feeling. You’ve just finished a solid lesson: students were engaged, they made progress, behaviour was calm, yet the feedback form doesn’t quite reflect the success you felt in the room.

But here’s the issue: sometimes those things did happen but just not in that small window of the lesson that was observed. Or maybe, quite simply, it wasn’t the right moment for that particular strategy. Not every lesson suits “Turn and Talk.

Teachers are told to make our instructions to students clear, concise, and free from cognitive overload. However, the feedback they receive can be the complete opposite: dense, checklist-heavy, and packed with so many “next steps” that none of them truly land.

In the documentary The Great Teaching Unpacked by Steplab, there’s a great example of this: teachers and senior leaders role-play feedback together. They don’t just say “you could try narrating behaviour” — they act it out, together, in groups. This approach transforms feedback from something abstract and evaluative into something collaborative and developmental.
The best feedback isn’t a list of eight things to fix; it’s one actionable focus that a teacher can actually embed. Anything more than that adds unnecessary cognitive load and dilutes the impact.
When feedback is simplified, focused, and modelled live, it becomes empowering rather than overwhelming. Teachers leave the room feeling supported, not judged.

There are many brilliant schools in England where leaders genuinely care about staff wellbeing and professional growth. But sometimes, in their eagerness to help teachers improve, they accidentally create the very thing they warn against: cognitive overload.
